paper_sections.title: Differential patterns of cortical activation as a function of fluid reasoning complexity.
fMRI Subject Selection and Behavioral Task
Functional Differences Between High-gfand Low-gf Samples

description.value: The study investigated how fluid reasoning complexity and individual differences in fluid intelligence affect cortical BOLD activity, comparing high-gf and low-gf participants during figural and analytic reasoning tasks.

spans.text: Our first goal was verifying the probable presence of differential patterns of activation in response to increasing fluid difficulty which might depend on gf variability among individuals.

design.value: Two groups differing in fluid intelligence performed moderate figural, complex analytic, and control reasoning tasks during fMRI; activity was analyzed within and between groups.

spans.text: To further investigate this, two samples of participants (high-IQ, N = 8; low-IQ, N = 10) with significant differences in gf underwent two reasoning (moderate and complex) tasks and a control task adapted from the Raven progressive matrices.

For the fMRI session, we developed a computerized behavioral task composed by a total of 32 fluid reasoning and 32 control problems adapted from both the RSPM [Raven, 1976] and RAPM [Raven, 1965].

task_description.value: Participants solved 3 × 3 Raven-type matrices with a missing lower-right entry by selecting the best answer from eight alternatives; control matrices contained figural elements devoid of logical relations.

spans.text: Each reasoning problem consisted of a 3 × 3 matrix placed on the left visual field of the subject in which the bottom right entry was missing.
A scanning session consisted of two different runs (for a total of 32 trials), each made up of 8 figural, 8 analytic, and 16 control items.

interpretations.value: a distributed fronto-parietal network subserving fluid intelligence
